_link.title: I can describe the three memory stores in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following lists the three memory stores in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model in the correct order?

options.text: Sensory memory, short-term memory, long-term memory
options.explanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three stores in sequence: sensory memory, short-term memory (STM), and long-term memory (LTM).

options.text: Long-term memory, short-term memory, sensory memory
options.explanation: This reverses the correct order. Information flows from sensory memory to STM to LTM in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model.

options.text: Short-term memory, sensory memory, long-term memory
options.explanation: Sensory memory is the first store, not the second. The correct order is sensory memory, STM, LTM.

options.text: Episodic memory, semantic memory, procedural memory
options.explanation: These are types of long-term memory, not the three stores in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model.

toLevel2.stem: According to the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, each of the three memory stores differs in which two key properties?

options.text: Capacity and duration
options.explanation: The three stores — sensory memory, STM, and LTM — each have different capacities and durations.

options.text: Colour and brightness
options.explanation: Colour and brightness are not properties of memory stores. The stores differ in capacity and duration.

options.text: Location and temperature
options.explanation: Location and temperature are not properties of memory stores. The stores differ in capacity and duration.

options.text: Speed and frequency
options.explanation: Speed and frequency are not the key properties that distinguish the three stores. They differ in capacity and duration.

toLevel2.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, which memory store holds information for the briefest duration?

options.text: Sensory memory
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds information for the briefest duration — approximately 0.2 to 4 seconds depending on the sensory modality.

options.text: Short-term memory
options.explanation: STM holds information for approximately 18–30 seconds without rehearsal, which is longer than sensory memory.

options.text: Long-term memory
options.explanation: LTM has a relatively permanent duration, which is the longest of the three stores.

options.text: All stores hold information for equal durations
options.explanation: The three stores have different durations. Sensory memory is the briefest, followed by STM, then LTM.

toLevel2.stem: Which memory store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model holds the name of a person while you walk to the door?

options.text: Short-term memory
options.explanation: STM holds information temporarily — such as a person's name — for approximately 18–30 seconds while it is being actively used.

options.text: Sensory memory
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds very brief sensory impressions, not information being actively maintained like a person's name.

options.text: Long-term memory
options.explanation: LTM stores information over long periods, but temporarily holding a name while walking to the door is a function of STM.

options.text: Procedural memory
options.explanation: Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory for motor skills, not a store that temporarily holds names.

toLevel2.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, which memory store has a relatively permanent duration?

options.text: Long-term memory
options.explanation: LTM has a relatively permanent duration and stores information such as memories of people known for years.

options.text: Sensory memory
options.explanation: Sensory memory has the briefest duration of all three stores, not a relatively permanent duration.

options.text: Short-term memory
options.explanation: STM holds information for approximately 18–30 seconds without rehearsal, not for a relatively permanent duration.

options.text: All three stores have a permanent duration
options.explanation: Only LTM has a relatively permanent duration. Sensory memory and STM have much shorter durations.

toLevel2.stem: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three distinct memory stores: sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is correct. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three distinct stores — sensory memory, STM, and LTM — each with different capacities and durations.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model does propose three distinct stores: sensory memory, STM, and LTM.

toLevel2.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory all have the same capacity and duration.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Each of the three stores has different capacities and durations. They are distinct stores with unique properties.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is incorrect. The three stores have different capacities and durations — this is a key feature of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model.

toLevel2.stem: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three distinct stores: {{blank:1}} memory, short-term memory, and {{blank:2}} memory.
Each of the three stores in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model differs in {{blank:1}} and {{blank:2}}.
In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, {{blank:1}} memory holds the briefest sensory impressions, while {{blank:2}} memory has a relatively permanent duration.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best explains why the Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three separate stores rather than one unified store?

options.text: Each store has distinct capacity and duration properties, suggesting they operate as separate systems
options.explanation: The three stores differ in capacity and duration, which supports the idea that they are distinct systems rather than a single unified store.

options.text: All three stores have identical properties but are named differently for convenience only
options.explanation: The stores do not have identical properties. They differ in capacity and duration, which is why they are modelled as separate stores.

options.text: Only one store actually exists, and the model divides it artificially into three stages
options.explanation: The model proposes three distinct stores with different properties, not an artificial division of a single store.

options.text: The three stores were named after the three researchers who independently discovered memory
options.explanation: The model was proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin. The three stores are defined by their different capacities and durations, not named after researchers.

toLevel3.stem: A doorbell rings and you briefly hear the sound before it fades. You then hold the visitor's name in mind while walking to the door. Later that evening, you recall a childhood memory of the same visitor. Which of the following correctly matches each experience to its memory store?

options.text: Hearing the bell — sensory memory; holding the name — STM; recalling a childhood memory — LTM
options.explanation: The brief sensation of the doorbell is held in sensory memory, the visitor's name is held temporarily in STM, and the childhood memory is stored in LTM.

options.text: Hearing the bell — STM; holding the name — LTM; recalling a childhood memory — sensory memory
options.explanation: The brief sensation of the bell is sensory memory, not STM. Holding a name temporarily is STM, and childhood memories are in LTM.

options.text: Hearing the bell — LTM; holding the name — sensory memory; recalling a childhood memory — STM
options.explanation: This reverses the stores. Brief sensory impressions are sensory memory, temporary active information is STM, and long-standing memories are LTM.

options.text: All three experiences use the same store because they involve the same person and event
options.explanation: The stores are defined by their properties (capacity, duration), not by the content. Different aspects of the experience involve different stores.

toLevel3.stem: How does the Atkinson-Shiffrin model explain where information can be lost in the memory system?

options.text: Information can be lost at each store if it is not transferred to the next store
options.explanation: The model explains that information can be lost at any of the three stores — sensory memory, STM, or LTM — if it is not successfully transferred to the next stage.

options.text: Information can only be lost from LTM because the other stores are completely permanent
options.explanation: Information is more easily lost from sensory memory and STM due to their brief durations. All three stores can experience information loss.

options.text: Information cannot be lost from any store once it has entered the memory system initially
options.explanation: Information can be lost at each store. Sensory memory fades within seconds, and STM loses information within 18–30 seconds without rehearsal.

options.text: Information is only lost from sensory memory because STM and LTM are both permanent stores
options.explanation: STM also has limited duration (18–30 seconds) and information can be lost from it. Only LTM has a relatively permanent duration.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the three stores in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?

options.text: Information flows sequentially from sensory memory to STM to LTM through encoding processes
options.explanation: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, information flows sequentially through the three stores, with encoding processes transferring information from one store to the next.

options.text: The three stores operate completely independently with no transfer of information between them
options.explanation: The stores are connected. Information transfers from sensory memory to STM and from STM to LTM through encoding processes.

options.text: Information enters LTM first and is then distributed to sensory memory and STM as needed
options.explanation: Information enters sensory memory first, then may transfer to STM, and then to LTM — not the reverse.

options.text: All information enters all three stores simultaneously without any sequential processing
options.explanation: The model proposes sequential processing: information enters sensory memory first, then STM, then LTM.

toLevel3.stem: Why is understanding the three stores in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model important for explaining how memories are formed?

options.text: It provides a framework showing how information moves through the system and where it can be lost
options.explanation: Knowing the three stores and their properties allows explanation of how information moves through the memory system and where it can be lost at each stage.

options.text: It proves that all memories are permanently stored and can never be forgotten under any circumstances
options.explanation: The model actually shows how information can be lost at each store, not that all memories are permanently stored.

options.text: It demonstrates that memory is a single unified process with no distinct stages or properties
options.explanation: The model specifically proposes three distinct stores with different properties, not a single unified process.

options.text: It eliminates the need to study brain structures because the stores explain all memory processes
options.explanation: The model describes functional stores but does not eliminate the need to understand brain structures involved in memory.

toLevel3.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, what distinguishes short-term memory from the other two stores?

options.text: STM has limited capacity and a duration of approximately 18–30 seconds without rehearsal
options.explanation: STM is distinguished by its limited capacity (approximately 7±2 items) and brief duration (18–30 seconds without rehearsal), placing it between sensory memory and LTM.

options.text: STM has unlimited capacity and a relatively permanent duration like long-term memory
options.explanation: STM does not have unlimited capacity or permanent duration. It has limited capacity and a duration of approximately 18–30 seconds.

options.text: STM holds only sensory impressions for less than one second before they are discarded
options.explanation: This describes sensory memory, not STM. STM holds information for 18–30 seconds and processes it beyond raw sensory form.

options.text: STM is identical to sensory memory in both its capacity and its duration properties
options.explanation: STM and sensory memory have different capacities and durations. Sensory memory has a much briefer duration and larger capacity.

toLevel3.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, information flows sequentially from sensory memory through short-term memory to long-term memory, and can be lost at each stage.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Information does flow sequentially through the three stores, and it can be lost at each stage if not transferred to the next store.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model describes sequential flow through three stores, with potential loss at each stage.

toLevel3.stem: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model explains how information moves through the memory system and where it can be {{blank:1}} at each {{blank:2}}.
Sensory memory holds a brief sensation of a doorbell for up to 4 seconds, while {{blank:1}} holds a person's name for 18–30 seconds, and {{blank:2}} stores memories from years of knowing someone.
In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, information flows {{blank:1}} from sensory memory to STM to LTM through {{blank:2}} processes.

toLevel4.stem: Ava hears her teacher announce a phone number. She repeats it silently while searching for a pen, but by the time she finds one 40 seconds later, she has forgotten the number. Which aspect of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model best explains why Ava forgot?

options.text: The number was held in STM, which has a limited duration of 18–30 seconds, and was lost before transfer to LTM
options.explanation: STM holds information for approximately 18–30 seconds. Despite rehearsal, the 40-second delay exceeded STM's duration and the number was not transferred to LTM.

options.text: The number was stored in LTM but could not be retrieved because Ava was distracted by the pen search
options.explanation: The number was in STM, not LTM. STM's limited duration explains the forgetting, not a retrieval failure from LTM.

options.text: The number was held in sensory memory, which can only retain auditory information for up to 4 seconds
options.explanation: Ava was actively repeating the number, indicating it had moved beyond sensory memory into STM.

options.text: The number was permanently encoded in LTM but was displaced by the memory of searching for the pen
options.explanation: Displacement occurs in STM, not LTM. The number was lost from STM due to its limited duration, not displaced from LTM.

toLevel4.stem: During a lecture, James briefly sees a diagram on a screen before the slide changes. He cannot recall the details of the diagram. Which store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model most likely held the diagram, and why was it lost?

options.text: Sensory memory — the brief visual impression faded before it could be transferred to STM
options.explanation: The brief visual impression was held in sensory memory (iconic memory), which has a very short duration. Without attention, it faded before being transferred to STM.

options.text: LTM — the diagram was permanently stored but James cannot retrieve it due to interference
options.explanation: The diagram was not stored in LTM. The brief exposure meant it was only in sensory memory, which faded before transfer to STM.

options.text: STM — the diagram was rehearsed but displaced by new information from the next slide
options.explanation: James did not rehearse the diagram. The brief exposure suggests it was held only in sensory memory before fading.

options.text: All three stores simultaneously held the diagram but all failed at the same time
options.explanation: The diagram was only briefly seen, placing it in sensory memory. It did not reach STM or LTM before fading.

toLevel4.stem: Maya studies a list of historical dates over several weeks. Months later, she can recall most of them during an exam. Which store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is Maya retrieving the dates from?

options.text: Long-term memory
options.explanation: Information retained over months is stored in LTM, which has a relatively permanent duration. Maya's repeated study transferred the dates from STM to LTM.

options.text: Short-term memory
options.explanation: STM holds information for only 18–30 seconds. Information retained for months is stored in LTM.

options.text: Sensory memory
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds information for fractions of a second to a few seconds. Information retained for months is in LTM.

options.text: All three stores equally
options.explanation: Months-old information is stored in LTM specifically. Sensory memory and STM have much shorter durations.

toLevel4.stem: A researcher presents participants with a tone lasting 0.5 seconds and asks them to identify it immediately versus after a 10-second delay. Performance drops significantly after the delay. Which aspect of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model best explains this finding?

options.text: The tone was held in sensory memory, which fades within seconds, reducing accuracy after a 10-second delay
options.explanation: Echoic (auditory) sensory memory holds information for approximately 3–4 seconds. A 10-second delay exceeds this duration, explaining the performance drop.

options.text: The tone was stored in LTM but was displaced by new information during the 10-second delay period
options.explanation: A brief tone would be held in sensory memory, not LTM. The fading of sensory memory explains the performance drop.

options.text: The tone was permanently encoded but the participant's STM capacity was exceeded by the delay
options.explanation: The issue is not STM capacity but the fading of the sensory memory trace within seconds of the tone being presented.

options.text: The 10-second delay caused LTM to retroactively erase the sensory impression of the initial tone
options.explanation: LTM does not erase sensory impressions. The sensory memory trace simply faded within its normal duration of a few seconds.

toLevel4.stem: Tom is introduced to three new people at a party. He repeats their names silently but is then interrupted by a loud announcement. When the announcement ends 45 seconds later, he cannot recall any of the names. Which stores and processes in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model best explain this?

options.text: The names were in STM but the interruption prevented rehearsal, and STM's limited duration caused forgetting
options.explanation: The names were held in STM through rehearsal. The interruption stopped rehearsal, and STM's duration of 18–30 seconds was exceeded during the 45-second delay.

options.text: The names were permanently stored in LTM but the announcement created retroactive interference in LTM
options.explanation: The names were not yet in LTM. They were in STM and were lost when rehearsal was interrupted and STM's duration was exceeded.

options.text: The names were in sensory memory, which has unlimited capacity but was overwhelmed by the announcement
options.explanation: Tom was actively rehearsing the names, indicating they were in STM, not sensory memory.

options.text: The names were never encoded into any memory store because Tom was at a noisy party environment
options.explanation: Tom was silently rehearsing the names, indicating they were encoded into STM. The issue was that rehearsal was interrupted.

toLevel4.stem: A student can describe the Atkinson-Shiffrin model's three stores and their properties during a class discussion, even though she learned the model two years ago. Which property of LTM does this demonstrate?

options.text: LTM has a relatively permanent duration
options.explanation: The student's ability to recall information learned two years ago demonstrates LTM's relatively permanent duration — information can be stored and retrieved over long periods.

options.text: LTM has a duration of 18–30 seconds
options.explanation: A duration of 18–30 seconds describes STM, not LTM. LTM has a relatively permanent duration, as demonstrated by recall after two years.

options.text: LTM holds only sensory impressions
options.explanation: LTM stores many types of information, not only sensory impressions. The student's recall of conceptual knowledge demonstrates LTM's permanent duration.

options.text: LTM has the same limited capacity as STM
options.explanation: LTM has a potentially unlimited capacity, unlike STM's limited capacity. The relevant property here is LTM's relatively permanent duration.

toLevel4.stem: A psychologist tests a patient who can hold a phone number in mind for about 20 seconds but forgets it if distracted. The patient can also recall detailed childhood memories. Which conclusion is most consistent with the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?

options.text: The patient's STM and LTM are both functioning normally within their expected properties
options.explanation: Holding information for ~20 seconds is consistent with normal STM duration (18–30 seconds), and recalling childhood memories demonstrates intact LTM with relatively permanent duration.

options.text: The patient has impaired STM because they should be able to hold a phone number indefinitely
options.explanation: STM normally holds information for only 18–30 seconds. The patient's 20-second retention is within the normal range for STM.

options.text: The patient has impaired LTM because childhood memories should not be accessible after many years
options.explanation: LTM has a relatively permanent duration. Recalling childhood memories is consistent with normal LTM functioning.

options.text: The patient's sensory memory has replaced both STM and LTM as the primary memory store
options.explanation: Sensory memory cannot replace STM or LTM. The patient's performance is consistent with normal functioning of all three stores.

toLevel4.stem: When Ava heard a phone number and repeated it silently, the number was held in {{blank:1}}, but after 40 seconds it was lost because this store has a limited {{blank:2}}.
James briefly saw a diagram before the slide changed. The visual impression was held in {{blank:1}} memory, which faded before it could be transferred to {{blank:2}}.
Maya can recall historical dates months after studying them because her repeated study transferred the information from STM to {{blank:1}}, which has a relatively {{blank:2}} duration.

toLevel5.stem: A critic argues that the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is flawed because it treats the three stores as completely separate systems with no interaction. Which analysis of this criticism is most accurate?

options.text: The model does propose interaction — information flows between stores through encoding and retrieval processes
options.explanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model explicitly describes information flowing from sensory memory to STM to LTM through encoding, and from LTM back to STM through retrieval. The stores interact through these processes.

options.text: The criticism is entirely valid because the model states that no information can move between any of the stores
options.explanation: The model specifically describes sequential transfer of information between stores. The criticism misrepresents the model.

options.text: The model only allows interaction between sensory memory and LTM, completely bypassing STM
options.explanation: The model proposes sequential flow through all three stores: sensory memory to STM to LTM. STM is not bypassed.

options.text: The criticism is irrelevant because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model only describes a single unified memory store
options.explanation: The model explicitly proposes three distinct stores, not a single unified store. The criticism addresses the relationship between these stores.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proves that all information must pass through sensory memory and STM before reaching LTM, with no exceptions.' Which evaluation is most accurate?

options.text: The model proposes this sequence, but some evidence suggests certain information may reach LTM without full STM processing
options.explanation: While the model proposes sequential flow through all three stores, research on flashbulb memories and implicit learning suggests some information may be encoded into LTM without extensive STM processing.

options.text: The student is entirely correct because the model has been proven to account for every aspect of human memory
options.explanation: No model accounts for every aspect of human memory. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model is a useful framework but has recognised limitations.

options.text: The student is entirely incorrect because the model states information enters LTM first and then moves to STM
options.explanation: The model does propose the sequence sensory memory → STM → LTM. The student's description of the sequence is correct, but the claim of no exceptions is too strong.

options.text: The student is correct because sensory memory has unlimited capacity, ensuring all information enters the system
options.explanation: While sensory memory does have large capacity, the issue is whether all information must sequentially pass through STM before reaching LTM, which may have exceptions.

toLevel5.stem: Patient H.M. had his hippocampus surgically removed and could not form new long-term memories, yet his sensory memory and short-term memory remained intact. Which analysis of this case is most consistent with the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?

options.text: It supports the model by demonstrating that the stores are distinct systems that can be independently impaired
options.explanation: H.M.'s case shows that STM and sensory memory can function normally while LTM formation is impaired, supporting the model's proposal of three distinct stores.

options.text: It contradicts the model because the model predicts that damage to one store must impair all three stores
options.explanation: The model proposes three distinct stores, so selective impairment of one store is consistent with, not contradictory to, the model.

options.text: It is irrelevant to the model because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model does not address brain structures at all
options.explanation: While the model is primarily functional, evidence from brain damage cases like H.M. can be used to evaluate whether the stores are truly distinct.

options.text: It contradicts the model because H.M. should have lost all memory function including sensory and short-term
options.explanation: The model proposes distinct stores, so damage affecting LTM formation does not necessarily impair sensory memory or STM.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes replacing the Atkinson-Shiffrin model with a single-store model that treats all memory as one continuous system with varying levels of activation. Which evaluation is most balanced?

options.text: A single-store model may explain some findings but loses the explanatory power of distinct stores with different capacities and durations
options.explanation: The distinct capacity and duration properties of each store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model explain many memory phenomena. A single-store model would need to account for these differences through other mechanisms.

options.text: The single-store model is clearly superior because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model has no supporting evidence at all
options.explanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model is supported by substantial evidence, including differential capacity and duration findings and neuropsychological case studies like H.M.

options.text: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model is clearly superior and no alternative model could ever explain memory more effectively
options.explanation: While the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is influential, no model is beyond improvement. A balanced evaluation considers strengths and limitations of both approaches.

options.text: Both models are equally unsupported because memory cannot be studied scientifically using any framework
options.explanation: Memory can be studied scientifically. Both the Atkinson-Shiffrin model and alternative models are supported by research evidence.

toLevel5.stem: A study finds that participants can recall the gist of a briefly presented sentence even though they cannot recall the exact words. Which analysis of this finding in relation to the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is most accurate?

options.text: It suggests that some semantic processing occurs before information fully enters STM, which the model's strict sequential flow may not fully explain
options.explanation: The model proposes sequential flow, but recalling gist without exact words suggests meaning is extracted during or before STM processing, which may challenge a strict interpretation of the sequential flow.

options.text: It perfectly supports the model because sensory memory stores the meaning of sentences permanently
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds raw sensory impressions, not meaning. The finding raises questions about where semantic processing occurs in the sequential flow.

options.text: It is entirely irrelevant to the model because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model does not address language at all
options.explanation: The model addresses how all types of information move through memory stores, including verbal information.

options.text: It disproves the model completely because no information should ever transfer between any of the three stores
options.explanation: The model explicitly describes transfer between stores. The finding raises a nuanced question about the nature of processing, not about whether transfer occurs.

toLevel5.stem: A psychology teacher tells students: 'The Atkinson-Shiffrin model is outdated and should no longer be taught because newer models exist.' Which evaluation of this claim is most justified?

options.text: The model remains a valuable foundational framework despite limitations, and newer models build on rather than replace it
options.explanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model provides an important foundational framework for understanding memory stores and processes. Newer models often extend or refine it rather than completely replacing it.

options.text: The teacher is entirely correct because the model has no value and all its predictions have been disproven
options.explanation: Many of the model's core predictions about distinct stores with different properties have been supported by research. It remains a valuable teaching framework.

options.text: The teacher is entirely incorrect because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model perfectly explains every aspect of memory
options.explanation: No model perfectly explains all aspects of memory. The model has known limitations but remains a valuable foundational framework.

options.text: The teacher should only teach the model to students who have already mastered every newer model of memory
options.explanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model is typically taught as a foundational framework before introducing newer models, not after mastering them.

toLevel5.stem: Research shows that people who are experts in a domain (e.g., chess) can hold more domain-specific items in STM than non-experts. Which analysis of this finding in relation to the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is most accurate?

options.text: Experts use existing LTM knowledge to chunk information, effectively increasing the amount held in STM without changing its capacity
options.explanation: Experts can chunk domain-specific information using their extensive LTM knowledge, allowing more information to be held within STM's limited capacity. This involves interaction between STM and LTM.

options.text: Experts have a biologically larger STM capacity that allows them to hold more items than non-experts
options.explanation: STM capacity is generally consistent across individuals. Experts use chunking strategies supported by LTM knowledge, not a larger biological STM.

options.text: This finding disproves the model entirely because STM should have the same capacity for all individuals
options.explanation: STM does have a similar capacity for all, but chunking (supported by LTM) allows experts to hold more meaningful units within that capacity.

options.text: Experts bypass STM entirely and store all domain-specific information directly in sensory memory
options.explanation: Experts do not bypass STM. They use LTM-supported chunking to organise information within STM's normal capacity limits.

toLevel5.stem: Two students debate the Atkinson-Shiffrin model. Student A says the model is useful because it identifies distinct stores with measurable properties. Student B says the model is too simplistic because it does not account for different types of LTM. Which evaluation is most balanced?

options.text: Both students make valid points — the model's strength is its clear structure, but it does not differentiate between LTM subtypes
options.explanation: Student A correctly identifies the model's strength in proposing distinct stores with measurable properties. Student B correctly notes that the model treats LTM as a single store without distinguishing subtypes like episodic, semantic, and procedural memory.

options.text: Only Student A is correct because the model does account for all types of LTM including episodic and procedural
options.explanation: The original Atkinson-Shiffrin model treats LTM as a single store and does not differentiate between subtypes. Student B's criticism is valid.

options.text: Only Student B is correct because a model that does not account for LTM subtypes has no scientific value at all
options.explanation: A model can have scientific value even with limitations. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model's clear structure and measurable properties make it a valuable framework.

options.text: Neither student is correct because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model has been completely replaced by newer models of memory
options.explanation: The model has not been completely replaced. It remains a foundational framework, and both students raise valid points about its strengths and limitations.

toLevel5.stem: Patient H.M.'s intact STM but impaired LTM formation {{blank:1}} the Atkinson-Shiffrin model by demonstrating that the stores are {{blank:2}} systems.
A limitation of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is that it treats LTM as a single store without differentiating between {{blank:1}} such as episodic, semantic, and procedural memory.
